Eye and ear protection

A shotgun shot is very loud: about 160–170 dB at the shooter's ear at its loudest instant. Decibels (dB) measure loudness, and a shot is an “impulse” sound: one short, sharp bang. For one such bang the upper limits are 140 dB for adults and 120 dB for children. The adult limit comes from workplace safety rules; the limit for children is recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). A shot is well over both limits, so even one unprotected shot can harm your hearing. Damage from noise builds up over time and usually does not go away. Ringing in the ears after shooting, called tinnitus, can be an early warning sign.

Well researched

Hearing protection is compulsory for everyone on or near a layout (the shooting area with its stands and traps): shooters, referees, staff and spectators. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ safety glasses are compulsory, without exception, for shooters, referees, staff and anyone close to a stand. In Compak® Sporting the glasses rule names competitors, referees and staff. A shooter who steps onto the stand without glasses or hearing protection is treated as absent, as if they had not turned up for their turn, and may not shoot. In Sporting™ the late-shooter rule then applies.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Children at the shooting ground, outside the clubhouse, wear hearing protection at all times.

Compak® Sporting

There is no separate line on children, but the rule covers all spectators near the layout, children included.

Eye protection matters just as much. Target fragments, pellets bouncing back from hard surfaces, twigs and dust can hit an eye.

For hearing protection there are two main types: earplugs, which sit in the ear canal, and ear muffs, which cover the ears. Simple passive muffs just block sound. Electronic ear muffs cut the bang but let voices through, so you still hear the referee.

Tip: Protection works only if it fits. Earplugs must sit deep and snug, and muffs must seal all round the ears. Custom-moulded plugs are comfortable and fit the same way each time, but well-inserted foam plugs also protect well. The SNR figure on the packaging (Single Number Rating, the product’s noise-reduction rating) shows how much it cuts noise: the higher, the more.

Some research

Earplugs and muffs together give the most protection. In tests on an acoustic dummy head, protection cut the peak of a shot by about 30 dB with earplugs or ear muffs alone and about 50 dB with both together. Hearing experts suggest wearing both with large-bore guns, such as the 12-gauge shotguns used at clay grounds, and whenever many shots are fired.

Some research

Shooting glasses are made of impact-resistant material, and many have interchangeable lenses. Many shooters find that a yellow or orange tint helps in dull light and a darker one in bright sun. If you wear glasses for your eyesight, ask about frames with prescription inserts. More in Shooting glasses and lens colours.

Clothing is part of safety too. Sandals are banned at FITASC competitions, and in Compak® Sporting at practice as well. Shorts are allowed only in the longer Bermuda style, ending no more than 5 cm above the knee. The competitor number is worn on the back, fully visible. The full dress code is in Dress code and safety on the stand.

Tip: Put protection on before you walk up to the stand, and check that you have both glasses and ear protection. Keep them on while anyone nearby is shooting. In training the shooting ground often lends glasses and earplugs; later it is worth having your own.

Key points

  • Ear protection for everyone near a layout, spectators and interpreters included
  • Glasses: Sporting™ — anyone close to a stand; Compak® Sporting — competitors, referees, staff
  • Without glasses or ear protection a shooter is treated as absent and may not shoot
  • Protection works only if it fits; plugs and muffs together protect most
  • Electronic muffs soften the shot but let voices through

Did you know?

Electronic ear muffs have small microphones: they pass quiet sounds such as voices through and turn the sound down at once when a shot is fired.

Stand Talk

  • Coach Eyes and ears on before you leave the clubhouse.

    Meaning: Put on glasses and hearing protection before walking out to the layouts.

  • Coach Where are your ears?

    Meaning: “Ears” = hearing protection, not the ears themselves.

  • Coach You can’t shoot in sandals here.

    Meaning: Closed shoes are required for safety.

  • Referee Your number’s folded — it has to be fully visible.

    Meaning: The competitor number on the back must be complete and visible; otherwise a warning.

For the interpreter
  • That includes you. Standing behind the stand, you are “near a layout”. Electronic ear muffs are a good choice for an interpreter: they soften the shot but let voices through, so you hear the coach and the referee. Clear or tinted shooting glasses also protect you from falling target fragments; a cap helps too.
  • Dress like a calm professional: closed shoes, neutral clothes and nothing that flaps or shines in the shooter’s eyes.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Who must wear hearing protection at a competition?

    1. Only the shooter who is on the stand
    2. Shooters and referees, but not spectators
    3. Everyone near the layout, spectators too
    Answer

    Everyone near the layout, spectators too

    The rules of both disciplines name shooters, referees, staff and spectators near the layout.

  2. Your shooter walks onto the stand without safety glasses. How do the rules treat him?

    1. He gets a warning and may shoot
    2. He may shoot if the coach agrees
    3. He loses one target
    4. He is treated as absent
    Answer

    He is treated as absent

    In both disciplines a shooter without eye or ear protection on the stand is treated as absent and may not shoot.

  3. Which gives the most hearing protection when many shots are fired?

    1. Earplugs and ear muffs worn together
    2. Electronic muffs with the volume turned up
    3. Earplugs pushed in loosely, for comfort
    Answer

    Earplugs and ear muffs worn together

    Plugs and muffs together protect most, as long as both fit well.
